name: Dental inlays and onlays

lead: Inlays and onlays are custom restorations made outside the mouth and bonded into a tooth. An inlay sits within the cusps of a molar or premolar; an onlay also covers one or more cusps. They are used when a filling is too small a repair but a crown would remove more tooth than needed.
For appearance, ceramic and composite versions match tooth colour closely, replacing old dark metal or failing fillings so the back teeth look natural when smiling or laughing.

paras: Traditionally the dentist prepares the tooth and takes an impression, a lab fabricates the piece, and it is bonded at a second visit. Chairside CAD-CAM systems can mill ceramic restorations in one visit.

Ceramic restorations can fracture, debond or develop decay at the margins; failure is more common in molars, root-canal-treated teeth and in people who grind their teeth. Preparation removes some healthy tooth structure, though less than a crown.

chain: Damaged back tooth is prepared conservatively
Custom ceramic or composite piece is bonded in
Tooth regains natural colour and shape without a full crown
angle.text: A tooth-coloured inlay or onlay replaces a large filling or fractured cusp so the tooth looks natural. Because it covers less than a crown, more of the original tooth is kept.

lead: Dental inlays and onlays are indirect restorations: the repair is fabricated outside the mouth, then cemented or bonded into a prepared tooth. They are used on molars and premolars where decay or fracture is too extensive for a direct filling [1].

Their cosmetic role is to restore a back tooth in a tooth-coloured material. Gold was long used for durability but is declining because it is visible; ceramic, composite and zirconia options allow close shade matching [1].
The first chairside CAD-CAM ceramic inlay was placed in 1985, and same-day systems became practical around 2000 [1].

paras: An inlay fills the area between cusps; an onlay extends over one or more cusps, and a crown covers the whole tooth. Onlays preserve more tooth structure than crowns [1].

Materials differ: gold is strong and gentle on opposing teeth; ceramics give good aesthetics and wear resistance but are more brittle; laboratory composite can be layered for shade and is easier to repair; zirconia is strong but needs careful handling [1].

In the traditional route the tooth is prepared, an impression is taken and a temporary is placed while a lab makes the final piece. CAD-CAM systems use an intraoral scan and milling to complete it in one visit. Restorations are bonded with resin cement [1].

Well-made gold inlays are very durable. Onlays most often fail by ceramic fracture, then debonding and secondary decay, and failure is higher in molars, root-canal-treated teeth and in patients who grind or clench [1].

Long-term studies reported in the dental literature show failure rates for ceramic or composite inlays that are not significantly higher than for direct composite fillings, though evidence is mixed [1].
Porcelain inlays were first described in 1857, chairside CAD-CAM ceramic inlays began in 1985 and CEREC 3 launched in 2000 [1].
